708.title: The altar of witness (Joshua 22)
708.hook: a misunderstood altar nearly starts a war, until people talk
708.howItsDone: Jews read Joshua 22 as part of the Former Prophets, and teachers often turn to it as a story about suspicion between communities and the conversation that ended it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Caleb at eighty-five, asking for the hill country. Your line was give me this mountain. Did you take a first step? Today, an altar by the river, and a war that almost happens. Day seven hundred eight.

The soldiers are finally going home. For a long time the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh have fought beside everyone else, though their own land lies east of the Jordan. Joshua blesses them and sends them back across. At the river, they stop and build an altar. A big one, the text says, great to look at. Word reaches the other tribes, and the whole congregation gathers at Shiloh to go up to war against them. Brothers who just fought side by side are about to fight each other, over a pile of stones nobody has explained.
screen: `THE EASTERN TRIBES GO HOME.` → `A GREAT ALTAR BY THE JORDAN.` → `ISRAEL GATHERS FOR WAR.`

segments.voice: What the other tribes see looks like betrayal. In the Torah, offerings belong at the one place God chooses, and here is a second altar, built on the edge of the land. They remember Peor, where the people strayed, and Achan, whose sin brought trouble on everyone. So they're afraid the whole people will pay again. But before anyone draws a sword, they send people to talk. Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, goes with ten princes, one from each tribe. Their speech is an accusation, and it's also an offer: if your land feels unclean, come over and take a portion among us. Then the eastern tribes answer, and their answer begins with God's names, said twice, as if under oath: God knows, and Israel shall know. The altar was never meant for offerings. It was built out of fear. The Jordan runs between us, they say. One day your children might tell our children, you have no portion in the Lord. So we built a copy of the altar, a witness between us, so our children can point at it and say, we belong too. Phinehas hears it, and the mood turns at once. This day, he says, we know the Lord is among us. The army goes home. And the eastern tribes name the altar, and the name is a reason: "for it shall be a witness between us that the LORD is God." The Hebrew word for witness there is ed, and some translations call the altar Ed. Here is the irony. Each side was afraid of losing the other. The altar that nearly started a war was built to keep a family together, and nobody knew until somebody asked.
screen: `A SECOND ALTAR LOOKS LIKE BETRAYAL.` · `SEND PEOPLE TO TALK FIRST.` · `WE BUILT IT SO OUR CHILDREN BELONG.` · then, large: `ED: A WITNESS BETWEEN US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask before you assume. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing someone did lately that you've been reading the worst way: a short message, a silence, a change of plans, a door closed a bit too hard. Notice the story you've already written about it. Then, for the rest of the sit, write a second story, the way the eastern tribes might explain their altar. You don't have to believe it. Just hold both. Then shape one simple question you could ask them. The bell holds the time.
Ed. The altar by the Jordan that looked like rebellion, turned out to be a plea to belong, and was named as a witness. Today's word.
Your line: talk before you fight. Today, before you answer the thing that annoyed you, ask your one question first. Day seven hundred eight.

709.title: Choose this day (Joshua 24:15)
709.hook: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD"
709.howItsDone: Jews read Joshua 24, the covenant at Shechem and the death of Joshua, as the close of the book of Joshua; the chapter's retelling of history, starting with Terah, is studied alongside other passages where the people's story is told aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the altar by the Jordan that nearly started a war, and was named Ed. Your line was talk before you fight. Did you ask your question first? Today, Joshua's last gathering, and a choice. Day seven hundred nine.

Joshua's farewell begins with an awkward piece of family history. All the tribes are gathered at Shechem, elders, heads, judges, officers. And the story he tells starts further back than anyone might expect, before Abraham. Your fathers, he says, Terah, the father of Abraham, lived beyond the River, and served other gods. The people's history doesn't begin with faith. It begins with a man taken out of one life and led into another. Joshua tells it all, up to this moment. Then he stops, and asks the whole people to decide.
screen: `ALL THE TRIBES AT SHECHEM.` → `TERAH SERVED OTHER GODS.` → `THEN JOSHUA ASKS THEM TO DECIDE.`

segments.voice: For most of the speech, Joshua speaks in God's voice. I took your father Abraham. I sent Moses and Aaron. I brought you out. I gave you a land you didn't labor for, cities you didn't build, vineyards and olive groves you didn't plant. Everything they have arrives as a gift. Then Joshua speaks in his own voice. He urges them to serve the Lord and put away the other gods. And then, strangely, he hands them the choice anyway: if serving the Lord seems wrong to you, "choose you this day whom ye will serve." The gods your ancestors served beyond the River, or the gods of the land you live in now. And then he says where he stands: "but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." The people answer at once: far be it from us to forsake the Lord. Then Joshua pushes back. You can't serve the Lord, he says; he is a holy God. It sounds like he's trying to talk them out of it. Some readers hear a test: a choice made too quickly is easy to drop, so he makes them choose again, slowly. They do. No, they say, we will serve the Lord. Then you are witnesses against yourselves, he tells them, and they reply in one breath: we are witnesses. So a choice gets a date and a place. Joshua writes the words in a book, and sets up a great stone under the oak at Shechem, saying the stone has heard everything. Soon after, Joshua dies, and the book draws to a close. The choice isn't made once, for all time, by a leader. Each generation stands at its own Shechem.
screen: `I TOOK, I SENT, I GAVE: ALL OF IT A GIFT.` · `CHOOSE YOU THIS DAY.` · `YOU CAN'T: CHOOSE AGAIN, SLOWLY.` · then, large: `AS FOR ME AND MY HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: decide one thing for your household. Your house might be a family, a roommate, a partner, or just you and a kettle. Let one small question come up that keeps getting put off: when you eat together, how you speak when you're tired, what happens on the day of rest, who you call each week. Don't decide everything. Choose one thing, and say it inside, in Joshua's shape: as for me and my house, we will. Finish the sentence. The bell holds the time.
Shechem. Where Joshua gave his last words: here are the options, here is where I stand, now you decide, and decide again. Today's word.
Your line: the stone has heard everything. Today, tell one person in your house the thing you decided, so it has a witness. Day seven hundred nine.

what it means: Joshua urges, then hands them the choice, says where he stands, and pushes back when they agree too fast.
what a scholar hears: Joshua 24:2–13 is told in God's voice: I took, I sent, I gave; the choice comes only after the gift.

710.title: The cycle (Judges 2:11–19)
710.hook: the people stray, suffer, cry out, and a judge rescues them, again and again
710.howItsDone: Jews read Judges, Shoftim, among the Former Prophets, right after Joshua; its chapter two sets out the pattern of straying, oppression, crying out and rescue that the later stories follow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joshua at Shechem, and a choice made twice. Your line was the stone has heard everything. Did you tell someone what you decided? Today, a new book, and what happens to that choice. Day seven hundred ten.

A washing machine has a dial. Wash, rinse, spin, and round again to the start. The book of Judges has one too, and it shows it to you before the first story. Joshua is gone. His generation is gone. And the text says plainly that another generation arose after them, "which knew not the LORD." Nobody rebels in a single dramatic moment. People forget. And from that forgetting, the book sets its dial turning, and it keeps turning for chapter after chapter.
screen: `WASH, RINSE, SPIN, AND ROUND AGAIN.` → `A GENERATION WHICH KNEW NOT THE LORD.` → `THE DIAL STARTS TURNING.`

segments.voice: Chapter two lays out the whole pattern in a few verses, like a summary on the back of a book. First, the people stray: they serve the gods of the land and forsake the Lord who brought them out of Egypt. Second, they suffer: they're handed over to raiders and enemies, and they're greatly distressed. Third, they cry out: the passage calls it their groaning. Fourth, the Lord raises up a shofet, and the shofet saves them. And then the turn: when the shofet dies, they go back, the text says, and do worse than their fathers. Then the dial comes round again. Shofet is today's word. It's usually translated judge, and the book is called Shoftim, Judges. But in this book a shofet is mostly not someone in a courtroom. The text says the Lord raised up judges who delivered them out of the hand of those who plundered them. A shofet is a rescuer, raised up in a crisis, who leads while they live. Two details in the passage are worth slowing down for. The first: why does God send a rescuer? The text doesn't say the people repented. It says the Lord was moved by their groaning, because of those who oppressed and crushed them. The help comes in answer to pain, before anyone has changed. The second: the cycle isn't a perfect circle. When each judge dies, the text says, the people turn back and act more corruptly than their fathers. Each time round, a little lower. That's what keeps the book from being simply repetitive. It's a pattern you can watch, and name, and, once you see it, start to recognize in other places.
screen: `STRAY, SUFFER, CRY OUT.` · `A SHOFET IS RAISED UP AND SAVES.` · `MOVED BY THEIR GROANING.` · then, large: `EACH TIME ROUND, A LITTLE LOWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one cycle you repeat. Let one pattern in your own life come to mind, small is fine: the late night that leads to the bad morning, the argument that always starts the same way, the promise to yourself that fades by the weekend. Walk it through its stages, the way chapter two does. Where does it start? What's the forgetting? Where does it hurt? What do you do when it does? Don't try to fix it now. Just see the dial. The bell holds the time.
Shofet. Judge, in the book of Judges: a rescuer the Lord raises up when the people cry out, who leads them while they live. Today's word.
Your line: the cycle repeats. Today, when your pattern starts its first turn, name the stage you're in, out loud or in your head. Day seven hundred ten.

711.title: Ehud, left-handed (Judges 3:12–30)
711.hook: a left-handed man hides his sword where no one checks
711.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Ehud as part of Judges, among the Former Prophets; it follows soon after chapter two sets out the cycle of straying and rescue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shofet, and the dial of Judges: stray, suffer, cry out, rescue. Your line was the cycle repeats. Did you catch your pattern at its first turn? Today, the dial turns, and a rescuer arrives. Day seven hundred eleven.

A short blade, two-edged, about a cubit long. A man straps it to his right thigh, under his clothes, and walks toward the palace of a king. He's carrying tribute, the payment his people owe to Moab. Nobody stops him. A man bringing gifts to a king is easy to wave through. The book has already told us the one thing about him that matters here: "Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded."
screen: `A TWO-EDGED BLADE, A CUBIT LONG.` → `STRAPPED TO THE RIGHT THIGH.` → `A MAN LEFTHANDED.`

segments.voice: The dial from yesterday turns exactly as promised. Israel does evil again. Eglon, king of Moab, takes the city of palm trees, and Israel serves him for eighteen years. They cry out, and the Lord raises up a deliverer. And the deliverer's introduction is not his strength, his family's fame or his faith. It's his left hand. The text doesn't explain why that matters. Some readers suggest guards would check a fighter's left side, where a right-handed man wears his sword; the story only tells us where Ehud hid his. Then it slows down. Ehud delivers the tribute and leaves with the men who carried it. At the carved stones near Gilgal he sends them on, turns back alone, and says to the king: I have a secret word for you. The king sends everyone out. Alone in the king's private upper room, Ehud says: I have a message from God for you. The king rises from his seat, and with his left hand Ehud draws the blade. The text tells the rest plainly and briefly, and so will we: the king falls, Ehud locks the doors and slips out, and the servants wait outside, embarrassed, assuming the king needs privacy, until it's far too late. By then Ehud is in the hill country of Ephraim, blowing the shofar. Follow me, he calls, and the people take the fords of the Jordan, and the land has rest. A man introduced by one overlooked detail goes where no one thinks to look. The thing that set him apart is the very thing that let him through.
screen: `THE DIAL TURNS: MOAB RULES.` · `THE DELIVERER'S DETAIL: LEFT-HANDED.` · `A SECRET WORD, A MESSAGE FROM GOD.` · then, large: `WHERE NO ONE THINKS TO LOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use what others overlook in you. Bring to mind one thing about you that people tend to miss or count against you: being quiet, being young, being new, an accent, a different way of seeing, a skill nobody asks about. Hold it for a moment without apologizing for it. Then ask: where could this be exactly what's needed? One room, one problem, one person. Let a picture come. The bell holds the time.
Ehud. Son of Gera, of Benjamin, a man lefthanded: the judge raised up when Israel cried out, who carried a blade where no one checked and blew the shofar on the hills of Ephraim. Today's word.
Your line: left-handed. Today, offer the thing about you that usually gets overlooked, once, where it might help. Day seven hundred eleven.

712.title: Deborah under the palm tree (Judges 4:4–5)
712.hook: a prophetess judges Israel from beneath her own palm tree
712.tomorrow: I will surely go with thee (Judges 4:6–10)
712.howItsDone: Jews read Deborah's story in Judges 4 and 5, and the Talmud discusses her among the women it calls prophetesses; the chapters are also read in synagogue as a haftarah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ehud, the man nobody checked. Your line was left-handed. Did you offer the thing about you that gets overlooked? Today, a judge who sits still, and people come to her. Day seven hundred twelve.

Between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim, there's a palm tree with a name. People walk up the road to it, carrying, we can only guess, the usual things: a boundary stone that moved, a debt, a quarrel between neighbors. Under the tree sits a woman. The times are hard. After Ehud, the dial of Judges has turned again, and a Canaanite king named Jabin has pressed Israel hard, with a captain called Sisera and his chariots of iron. And in the middle of all that, the book stops to show us a woman under a tree, listening.
screen: `A PALM TREE WITH A NAME.` → `PEOPLE WALK UP WITH ARGUMENTS.` → `A WOMAN UNDER THE TREE, LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Here's how the text introduces her: "And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time." Three things in one breath. She's a prophetess. She's married. And she judges. Remember the word shofet, from two days ago? Ehud was a rescuer with a blade. Deborah is a judge in the sense the word sounds like. She hears cases. The next verse says where: under the palm tree of Deborah, "and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment." She doesn't travel the country. She doesn't summon anyone, not yet. People come up to her. Tradition has asked about the details. A teaching in the Talmud links the name Lapidoth to torches, and says she made wicks for the lamps of the sanctuary. The same teaching asks why a palm tree, and suggests she judged in the open air, where anyone could see, rather than alone behind a closed door. The Talmud also counts her among seven women it calls prophetesses. The text itself stays short. Two verses, and then the story moves on. But those two verses describe a different kind of leadership from Ehud's: no army, no hidden blade, just a place people know to go when they need someone wise and willing to listen. In a book full of cycles and crises, a tree where people bring their quarrels is its own kind of rescue. Before the battle that's coming, there's this: a woman known for her judgment, sitting where everyone can find her.
screen: `A PROPHETESS, A WIFE, A JUDGE.` · `THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL CAME UP TO HER.` · `TORCHES, WICKS, AND OPEN AIR.` · then, large: `DEBORAH JUDGED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give counsel when it's asked. Bring to mind someone who has brought you a problem lately, or might soon: a friend, a colleague, a child, a parent. Before any advice, picture just listening, the way people walked up the road to Deborah and found her already sitting there. What would they need to say first? What question could you ask before you answer? If no one comes to mind, think of who you would walk up the road to. The bell holds the time.
shofet. The word for judge that fits Deborah, a prophetess who judged Israel in the hill country of Ephraim, where the people came up to her for judgment. Today's word.
Your line: deborah judged. Today, when someone brings you a problem, listen all the way to the end before you answer. Day seven hundred twelve.

screen: `DAY 712 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: I WILL SURELY GO WITH THEE.`

713.title: I will surely go with thee (Judges 4:6–10)
713.hook: Barak won't go into battle without her, and she goes
713.howItsDone: Jews read Deborah and Barak's story in Judges 4, and the exchange between them is discussed in commentary, with readers differing over whether Barak's condition shows weakness or faith in the prophet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Deborah under the palm tree, a shofet where people came up to her for judgment. Your line was deborah judged. Did you listen all the way to the end? Today, she sends for someone. Day seven hundred thirteen.

"If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go." That's a soldier talking, to a judge. His name is Barak, son of Abinoam, and he's just been handed a war. Deborah has sent for him from Kedesh in Naphtali. The Lord has commanded, she tells him: gather ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor, and Sisera and his chariots will be drawn to you at the river Kishon. Barak hears all of it, and puts one condition on the table: you.
screen: `IF THOU WILT GO WITH ME, I WILL GO.` → `TEN THOUSAND AT MOUNT TABOR.` → `ONE CONDITION: YOU.`

segments.voice: Notice how Deborah delivers the call. She doesn't say, I've decided. She asks a question: hasn't the Lord, the God of Israel, commanded you? As if Barak already knows, and needs someone to say it out loud. And Barak's answer has been read in very different ways. Some readers hear fear, or a lack of faith: the Lord promised victory, and he still wants a person beside him. Others hear something wiser: he won't go without the prophet, the one through whom the word came. The text doesn't decide for us. What it does show is Deborah's answer, and it's surprisingly short. No lecture. No be brave, go alone. Just this: "I will surely go with thee." Then, in the same breath, an honest cost. The journey won't be for your honor, she says, "for the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Which woman? Some readers assume Deborah. The text doesn't say, not yet. And then the plain line that ends this little scene: Barak calls up Zebulun and Naphtali, ten thousand men go up behind him, "and Deborah went up with him." She had a tree, a court, a life where people came to her. She leaves it to walk beside the man who asked her to come, toward an army of iron chariots. She doesn't fight for him. She doesn't shame him. She goes.
screen: `HATH NOT THE LORD COMMANDED?` · `FEAR, OR WISDOM? THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY.` · `INTO THE HAND OF A WOMAN.` · then, large: `AND DEBORAH WENT UP WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go with someone who's afraid. Bring to mind someone facing something hard soon: a doctor's appointment, an exam, a difficult conversation, a first day. Picture them asking, quietly, will you come? Notice your first reaction, whatever it is. Then picture what going would look like in real life: sitting in the waiting room, a phone call before and after, a message the morning of. Choose one. The bell holds the time.
Barak. The soldier who told Deborah he wouldn't go to war without her, and her short, surprising answer: I will surely go with thee. Today's word.
Your line: I will go with you. Today, say it to someone facing something hard, and mean the part where you actually show up. Day seven hundred thirteen.

714.title: Jael (Judges 4:17–22, 5:24)
714.hook: the woman of the tent ends the war; her song calls her blessed above women in the tent
714.howItsDone: Jews read Jael's story in Judges 4 and her praise in the Song of Deborah in Judges 5, and commentators discuss how to understand her welcome of Sisera.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Deborah's answer to Barak. Your line was I will go with you. Did you say it to someone, and show up? Today, the woman Deborah spoke of, and she isn't Deborah. Day seven hundred fourteen.

The battle is lost, the army is broken, and the great captain is running on foot. Sisera, who had oppressed Israel with chariots of iron, has jumped down from his own and fled. He's heading for safety: the tent of Heber the Kenite, whose house is at peace with his king. A woman steps out of the tent to meet him. "Turn in, my lord, turn in to me; fear not." Her name is Jael. Deborah said the Lord would sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. The story has been waiting to show whose.
screen: `THE CAPTAIN RUNS ON FOOT.` → `A TENT AT PEACE WITH HIS KING.` → `TURN IN, MY LORD; FEAR NOT.`

segments.voice: Jael is an outsider to the story. She's the wife of Heber the Kenite, from a household that had moved away from its kin and made peace with Israel's enemy. She has no army, no title, no prophecy. She has a tent. And the text tells what happens inside it slowly, almost gently. She covers Sisera with a blanket. He asks for a little water; she opens a skin of milk and gives him a drink, and covers him again. He tells her to stand at the door: if anyone asks, is there a man here, say no. He falls asleep, worn out. Then she takes a tent peg and a hammer, the tools of her own home, and the war ends in her tent. When Barak arrives in pursuit, she goes out to meet him: come, I'll show you the man you're looking for. Deborah's words come true, with a woman nobody in the story was watching. This is a hard story, and readers have felt both sides of it. Some are troubled: she welcomed him, said fear not, gave him milk, and then killed him. Others see a woman who ended a long oppression with the only tools in reach. The text itself gives the last word to a song. In it Deborah and Barak sing: "Blessed above women shall Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite be, blessed shall she be above women in the tent." Not above women in palaces. Above women in the tent. Her place, the one nobody counted, is where the song blesses her.
